section.heading: 13.2. Derivatives and Integrals of Vector Functions
section.paragraph: Later in this chapter we are going to use vector functions to describe the motion of planets and other objects through space. Here we prepare the way by developing the calculus of vector functions.
section.heading: Derivatives
section.paragraph: The derivative $$\mathbf{r}^{\prime}$$ of a vector function $$\mathbf{r}$$ is defined in much the same way as for real-valued functions:
$$\frac{d\mathbf{r}}{\mathit{dt}} = \mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t) = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{\mathbf{r}\left( t + h) - \mathbf{r}\left( t) \right. \right.}{h}$$

if this limit exists. The geometric significance of this definition is shown in Figure 1. If the points $$P$$ and $$Q$$ have position vectors $$\mathbf{r}\left( t) \right.$$ and $$\mathbf{r}\left( {t + h}) \right.$$ , then $$\overset{\rightarrow}{PQ}$$ represents the vector $$\mathbf{r}\left( {t + h}) \right. - \mathbf{r}\left( t) \right.$$ , which can therefore be regarded as a secant vector. If $$h > 0$$ , the scalar multiple $$\left( {1 \slash h}) \right.\left( {\mathbf{r}\left( {t + h}) \right. - \mathbf{r}\left( t) \right.}) \right.$$ has the same direction as $$\mathbf{r}\left( {t + h}) \right. - \mathbf{r}\left( t) \right.$$ . As $$\left. h\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ , it appears that this vector approaches a vector that lies on the tangent line. For this reason, the vector $$\mathbf{r}^{\prime}\left( t) \right.$$ is called the tangent vector to the curve defined by $$\mathbf{r}$$ at the point $$P$$ , provided that $$\mathbf{r}^{\prime}\left( t) \right.$$ exists and $$\mathbf{r}^{\prime}\left( t) \right. \neq 0$$ . The tangent line to $$C$$ at $$P$$ is defined to be the line through $$P$$ parallel to the tangent vector $$\mathbf{r}^{\prime}\left( t) \right.$$ .
Notice that when $$0 < h < 1$$ , multiplying the secant vector by $$1 \slash h$$ stretches the vector, as shown in Figure 1(b).

section.paragraph: The following theorem gives us a convenient method for computing the derivative of a vector function $$\mathbf{r}$$ : just differentiate each component of $$\mathbf{r}$$ .

note.paragraph: If $$\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle f(t),g(t),h(t)\rangle = f(t)\mathbf{i} + g(t)\mathbf{j} + h(t)\mathbf{k}$$ , where $$f$$ , $$g$$ , and $$h$$ are differentiable functions, then

note.title: Proof
note.heading: Proof
note.paragraph: $$\begin{array}{l} {\mathbf{r}^{\prime}\left( t) \right. = \lim\limits_{\Delta t\rightarrow 0}\frac{1}{\Delta t}\left\lbrack {\mathbf{r}\left( {t + \Delta t}) \right. - \mathbf{r}\left( t) \right.} \right\rbrack} \\ {\phantom{\mathbf{r}^{\prime}\left( t) \right.} = \lim\limits_{\Delta t\rightarrow 0}\frac{1}{\Delta t}\left\lbrack {\langle{f\left( {t + \Delta t}) \right.,g\left( {t + \Delta t}) \right.,h\left( {t + \Delta t}) \right.}\rangle} - {\langle{f\left( t) \right.,g\left( t) \right.,h\left( t) \right.}\rangle} \right\rbrack} \\ {\phantom{\mathbf{r}^{\prime}\left( t) \right.} = \lim\limits_{\Delta t\rightarrow 0}\langle\frac{f\left( {t + \Delta t}) \right. - f\left( t) \right.}{\Delta t},\frac{g\left( {t + \Delta t}) \right. - g\left( t) \right.}{\Delta t},\frac{h\left( {t + \Delta t}) \right. - h\left( t) \right.}{\Delta t}\rangle} \\ {\phantom{\mathbf{r}^{\prime}\left( t) \right.} = \langle\lim\limits_{\Delta t\rightarrow 0}\frac{f\left( {t + \Delta t}) \right. - f\left( t) \right.}{\Delta t},\lim\limits_{\Delta t\rightarrow 0}\frac{g\left( {t + \Delta t}) \right. - g\left( t) \right.}{\Delta t},\lim\limits_{\Delta t\rightarrow 0}\frac{h\left( {t + \Delta t}) \right. - h\left( t) \right.}{\Delta t}\rangle} \\ {\phantom{\mathbf{r}^{\prime}\left( t) \right.} = {\langle{f^{\prime}\left( t) \right.,g^{\prime}\left( t) \right.,h^{\prime}\left( t) \right.}\rangle}} \end{array}$$

section.paragraph: A unit vector that has the same direction as the tangent vector is called the unit tangent vector $$\mathbf{T}$$ and is defined by
$$\mathbf{T}\left( t) \right. = \frac{\mathbf{r}^{\prime}\left( t) \right.}{\left| {\mathbf{r}^{\prime}\left( t) \right.} \right|}$$

(b) Find the unit tangent vector at the point where $$t = 0$$ .

section.paragraph: Just as for real-valued functions, the second derivative of a vector function $$\mathbf{r}$$ is the derivative of $$\mathbf{r}^{\prime}$$ , that is, $$\mathbf{r}^{''} = {(\mathbf{r}^{\prime})}^{\prime}$$ . For instance, the second derivative of the function in Example 3 is
$$\mathbf{r}^{''}{(t)} = {\langle{- 2\cos t, - \sin t,0}\rangle}$$

In Section 13.4 we will see how $$\mathbf{r}^{\prime}{(t)}$$ and $$\mathbf{r}^{''}{(t)}$$ can be interpreted as the velocity and acceleration vectors of a particle moving through space with position vector $$\mathbf{r}{(t)}$$ at time $$t$$ .

section.heading: Integrals
section.paragraph: The definite integral of a continuous vector function $$\mathbf{r}{(t)}$$ can be defined in much the same way as for real-valued functions except that the integral is a vector. But then we can express the integral of $$\mathbf{r}$$ in terms of the integrals of its component functions $$f$$ , $$g$$ , and $$h$$ as follows. (We use the notation of Chapter 5.)

$$\begin{array}{l} {\int_{a}^{b}\mathbf{r}(t)dt = \lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\underset{i=1}{\overset{n}{\sum}}\mathbf{r}\left( t_{i}^{\ast} \right)\Delta t} \\ {\phantom{\int_{a}^{b}\mathbf{r}(t)dt} = \lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left\lbrack \left( \left. {\underset{i=1}{\overset{n}{\sum}}f}{\left( t_{i}^{\ast} \right)\Delta t} \right)\mathbf{i} + \left( {{\underset{i=1}{\overset{n}{\sum}}g}\left( t_{i}^{\ast} \right)\Delta t} \right)\mathbf{j} + \left( {{\underset{i=1}{\overset{n}{\sum}}h}\left( t_{i}^{\ast} \right)\Delta t} \right)\mathbf{k} \right. \right\rbrack} \end{array}$$
and so
$$\int_{a}^{b}{\mathbf{r}(t) dt = \left( {\int_{a}^{b}{f(t) dt}} \right)\mathbf{i} + \left( {\int_{a}^{b}{g(t) dt}} \right)\mathbf{j} + \left( {\int_{a}^{b}{h(t) dt}} \right)\mathbf{k}}$$
This means that we can evaluate an integral of a vector function by integrating each component function.
We can extend the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus to continuous vector functions as follows:
$${\int_{a}^{b}\mathbf{r}}{(t)}dt = \mathbf{R}{(t)}\rbrack_{a}^{b} = \mathbf{R}{(b)} - \mathbf{R}{(a)}$$

where $$\mathbf{R}$$ is an antiderivative of $$\mathbf{r}$$ , that is, $$\mathbf{R}^{\prime}{(t)} = \mathbf{r}{(t)}$$ . We use the notation $$\int\mathbf{r}{(t)}dt$$ for indefinite integrals (antiderivatives).
